lesson.title: Robes and Rallies: The Klan's Second Life in the 1920s
lesson.summary: A refounded Ku Klux Klan exploded into a nationwide movement in the 1920s, broadening its original targeting of Black Americans into a wider crusade against Catholics, Jews, and immigrants before an internal scandal helped bring it down.
lesson.body:
The Ku Klux Klan that terrorized the Reconstruction-era South was not the only Klan in American history. In 1915, William J. Simmons founded a new Klan at Stone Mountain, Georgia, drawing on nostalgia for the original organization and on the popularity of D. W. Griffith's 1915 film "The Birth of a Nation," which romanticized the Reconstruction Klan as a heroic defender of white southern society. This second Klan started small, but it would grow into something far larger and more geographically widespread than its predecessor.

The two Klans differed in an important way. The Reconstruction-era Klan, covered in an earlier chapter, focused almost entirely on terrorizing newly freed Black Americans and their white allies in the South to restore white political control. The 1920s Klan kept anti-Black racism at its core, but it broadened its list of enemies to include Catholics, Jews, and immigrants, groups it portrayed as un-American threats to Protestant, native-born values, echoing the same nativist fears driving the immigration quota laws of the same decade. It also was not confined to the South; some of its strongest chapters formed in Indiana, Ohio, Oregon, and other Midwestern and Western states.

The Klan's growth in the early to mid-1920s was striking. Historians' estimates of its peak membership vary considerably and remain disputed, but commonly cited figures place it somewhere between two and five million members around 1924 and 1925. It wielded real political power in some states, most notably Indiana, where Grand Dragon D. C. Stephenson helped elect sympathetic officials and effectively controlled much of state politics. The organization marched openly and with confidence, including a demonstration of tens of thousands of members down Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C., in August 1925.

That same year brought the scandal that broke the Klan's momentum. Stephenson was convicted in 1925 in connection with the death of Madge Oberholtzer, a case that exposed shocking hypocrisy in an organization that claimed to stand for morality and traditional values. The scandal, combined with internal corruption and infighting, caused membership and political influence to collapse sharply in the years that followed. The 1920s Klan never fully recovered its earlier scale, though its ideas and its habit of scapegoating immigrants and religious minorities left a lasting mark on the decade's politics.
